author: William Saville

title: A Song That Isn't a Promise
subtitle: A Lanternweald continuation
content:
Greg had written a song about a door.

That should not have surprised me.

He wrote songs about the ocean, broken-down cars, coffee that had gone cold, and once about a chair that was so uncomfortable it deserved a public apology. The door was part of our history now. So was the patched blanket folded in the back of his van, and the fact that we kept leaving places and coming back without treating every departure as the end.

The song was good.

That was the problem.

"Play the second verse again," I said.

Greg looked up from his guitar.

"I've done that three times."

"Four, if you count the version where you forgot the words."

"I was improvising."

"You rhymed door with floor."

"Classic songwriting technique."

He grinned and strummed the opening chord again. We were sitting on Starwake Pier beneath a string of lanterns, with the evening sea turning copper around the pilings. At the far end, two children were trying to teach a wooden toy boat to sail against the wind.

Greg began to sing.

The melody was warm and easy to remember. It reminded me of Beach City in the hour before sunset, when the boardwalk noise softened and the ocean seemed bigger than everything people had been worrying about.

Then he reached the line that made me look up.

One door, one heart, one place to stay.

He finished the verse and waited.

"Well?" he asked.

"It's pretty."

"Pretty good or pretty bad?"

"Greg."

His smile faded.

"Okay. Talk to me."

I rested my hands on the edge of the bench.

"Does that line mean what it sounds like?"

He looked down at the page.

"It's a song about home."

"I know. But it sounds like the kind of promise we talked about not making."

He read the line again. The pause went on long enough that a wave slapped the pier below us.

"Oh," he said.

"Yeah."

"I didn't mean it like that."

"I believe you."

He ran his thumb along the guitar's edge.

"Somebody at the car wash heard the first version and said it was romantic that I'd finally found the one person I needed."

I felt something cold settle behind my ribs.

"What did you say?"

"Nothing."

I looked at him.

"Not because I agreed," he said quickly. "I just didn't know what to say in front of the customers. And then it felt weird to correct it later."

"That's fair. It can be awkward."

He nodded, but I could see he was still waiting for the harder part.

"I don't want the story people tell about us to be that I changed my mind about polyamory because you were special enough," I said. "You *are* special to me. That's not what the word exclusive means."

Greg set the guitar down between his feet.

"I know."

"Do you?"

He looked toward the water.

"I think I know in my head. Sometimes my heart takes the scenic route."

I smiled despite myself.

"Well, it has a van."

He let out a breath.

"I've spent years telling myself it was okay when people left," he said. "Sometimes it was. Sometimes it wasn't. I don't always know the difference until afterward. I don't want to turn that into a rule that keeps you from loving the way you love."

I moved a little closer.

"You can still ask for reassurance."

"Then I want some." He swallowed. "If you go through another door, do you still want to come back and play terrible songs with me?"

"Yes."

"Even if I make you listen to the chair song again?"

"That's pushing it."

He laughed, and the tension shifted.

"But yes," I said. "I do. And I want us to keep making agreements instead of guessing. If something changes, we tell each other. If you want a date that's just ours, say so. If you need space, say that too."

He nodded. "And no letting rumors do the talking for us."

"Exactly."

Greg picked up his pencil and crossed out the line.

"How about 'a door that opens, a light that stays'?"

"Better."

"Still too sentimental?"

"Absolutely."

"Great. That's the brand."

We tried the new verse. He stumbled over the rhythm twice. I caught the beat with my hands on the bench, and he adjusted the melody until the words sounded like something he actually meant.

A little later, Iroh appeared with two cups of tea and an expression of mild curiosity.

"Are you rehearsing?" he asked.

"Negotiating with a chord," Greg said.

"A difficult task. Chords are often very stubborn."

"Finally, somebody understands."

Iroh set the cups on the bench and listened to a verse. He did not offer a verdict. He asked what Greg wanted the song to carry.

"The feeling of having somewhere I can go back to," Greg said. "Without saying it has to be the only place anybody goes."

Iroh thought about that.

"Then perhaps the melody should leave room at the end."

Greg considered the unfinished measure.

"That's actually good advice."

I pointed at Iroh. "Don't tell him. He'll start charging by the metaphor."

Iroh's smile deepened.

The tea warmed my hands. The lanterns turned on above us, one after another. People from the square began to gather near the little stage, drawn by the music without having been promised a performance.

Greg looked at them, then at me.

"Want to hear it all the way through?"

"I do."

He played.

This time, when he reached the new line, his voice steadied. The song did not claim that one person could replace everyone a heart had ever known. It was about the courage of making a place, keeping a light and coming back because you wanted to.

When he finished, a few people clapped. One of the children shouted that the song needed more frogs.

Greg took the criticism seriously.

"That's what the bridge is for," he told them.

The children cheered.

After the chairs were folded and the cups returned, we walked toward the Starwake Door with the guitar between us. A breeze lifted the edge of my sweater. Greg reached for my hand and waited until I took it.

"You know," he said, "it's still pretty romantic."

"The song?"

"The part where nobody has to lie."

I stopped beside the door. The brass latch was cool beneath my free hand. He turned to face me, his smile a little nervous.

"Can I kiss you?" he asked.

"Please."

His kiss was warm and slightly clumsy because the guitar kept bumping his leg. I leaned closer, laughing into his shoulder. He kissed me again, softer.

We did not need the pier to applaud.

Back in Beach City, the van waited under the streetlamp with the patched blanket folded where we'd left it. Greg asked whether I wanted to stay for a while.

I told him yes.

He opened the door. The rest of the evening belonged to us, not to the lyrics on a page.

In the morning, a small folded note sat on the dashboard.

NEW SONG RULE: CHECK WITH JASPER BEFORE PROMISING ANYTHING TO THE WHOLE UNIVERSE.

Underneath, he had added a little drawing of the world's worst chair.

I kept the note.
